usage: 돌다 is the natural verb; 모퉁이를 돌면 = once you round the corner
pointing it out when giving directions
narrow side-street corner, not a big intersection
examples: 모퉁이에 우체통이 있어요.
There's a mailbox on the corner.
모퉁이에 = at the corner; the simplest 'corner as a spot' use
저 모퉁이를 돌면 편의점이 보여요.
If you round that corner, you'll see a convenience store.
the everyday direction formula: 모퉁이를 돌면 + landmark 보이다
다음 모퉁이에서 오른쪽으로 꺾으세요.
Turn right at the next corner.
꺾다 = to make a sharp turn; what a local says guiding you on foot
nuance: 모퉁이 is the corner where a road bends or a building's wall turns — the spot you physically round while walking, pictured from the outside. The near-synonym is 모서리, but the dividing line matters: 모서리 is the sharp edge or corner of a solid object (책상 모서리 = the corner of a desk, 모서리에 부딪히다 = to bump into an edge), while 모퉁이 is a place in the street you move around. It is plain, everyday speech with no register issue, said freely to anyone. It collocates above all with 돌다 (모퉁이를 돌다) and appears as 모퉁이 가게 / 골목 모퉁이 as a landmark. The English-speaker pitfall: English uses one word 'corner' for both the street corner and a table corner, so learners reach for 모퉁이 when they bump a desk — but that edge is 모서리. Also note Koreans say 모퉁이를 돌다 with the object particle 를, not 'turn at the corner' word-for-word.

english: the opposite side (right across, facing you)
usage: to be on the opposite side
바로 stresses it is straight across
examples: 은행은 편의점 맞은편에 있어요.
The bank is across from the convenience store.
the core pattern: [landmark] 맞은편에 있다, with 에 marking location
제 맞은편에 앉으세요.
Sit across from me.
제 맞은편 = the side facing me; 맞은편 works for a person opposite you, not just buildings (note: 저랑 here would wrongly mean 'together with me')
식당이 우리 회사 바로 맞은편이라서 점심때 자주 가요.
The restaurant is right across from our office, so I go there a lot at lunch.
바로 = directly; real-life reason clause showing 맞은편 as a familiar spot
nuance: 맞은편 is the side that directly faces you, built from 맞다 ('to face / to fit') + 편 ('side'), so the image is two spots looking straight at each other across a road, a river, or a table. The near-synonym is 건너편, and the dividing line is subtle but real: 맞은편 stresses facing (it can describe the person seated opposite you), while 건너편 stresses the crossing you do to get there. In daily speech they overlap heavily and either is usually fine. Register is neutral — fine with anyone. It collocates as 바로 맞은편, 맞은편 건물, 역 맞은편. The English-speaker pitfall: 'opposite' in English also means 'contrary / reverse' (the opposite is true), but 맞은편 is strictly spatial — for the abstract opposite you need 반대 (반대로). Another trap is the particle: a place 'is on the opposite side' is 맞은편에 있어요, never 맞은편 있어요 with the 에 dropped.

english: the other side (across the road or river)
usage: to go to the other side
to see from the other side
the far side of the river
across a river or wide road
examples: 길 건너편에 약국이 있어요.
There's a pharmacy across the street.
길 건너편 = across the road, the single most common pairing
건너편으로 가려면 횡단보도를 건너세요.
To get to the other side, cross at the crosswalk.
으로 = toward; the verb 건너다 echoes the 건너 in 건너편
아까 강 건너편에서 불꽃놀이를 봤는데 진짜 예뻤어요.
Earlier I watched the fireworks from the far side of the river, and it was really pretty.
에서 = from that side; a lived-in scene showing the 'across a river' sense
nuance: 건너편 comes from the verb 건너다 ('to cross') + 편 ('side'), so it literally means 'the cross-over side' — the side you reach by crossing something: a road, a river, the tracks. That built-in crossing is what separates it from its near-synonym 맞은편: 건너편 foregrounds the act of getting across, while 맞은편 simply foregrounds facing you. For directions involving a 횡단보도 (crosswalk) or a wide road, locals reach for 건너편 first, and it pairs naturally with 건너다 (건너편으로 건너가다). Register is neutral. Common collocations: 길 건너편, 강 건너편, 건너편으로 가다. The English-speaker pitfall: English 'the other side' is vaguer than 건너편 — 'the other side of the room' is not 건너편 (use 반대쪽 for the far end of an enclosed space); 건너편 specifically implies a barrier you cross. Also do not confuse it with 다음 ('the next one along') — 건너편 is across from you, not the next building in a row.

usage: to cut through via the shortcut
examples: 이 길이 지름길이에요.
This road is a shortcut.
the simplest framing: [road] 이/가 지름길이다
지름길을 알면 십 분은 빨라요.
If you know the shortcut, it's a good ten minutes faster.
은 here softly emphasizes the amount; pairs the word with a time saving
성공에 지름길은 없다고 생각해요.
I think there's no shortcut to success.
the figurative 'fast track' sense — 성공의 지름길 is a set phrase
nuance: 지름길 is a native Korean compound, not Sino-Korean: from the verb 지르다 ('to cut straight across / take a direct line') + 길 ('road'), so it pictures the path that slices straight through instead of going the long way around. It means a shorter, faster route — often through alleys or back streets a local knows — and just as commonly it is figurative: 성공의 지름길 = 'the shortcut to success', a fast track to a goal. Its natural opposite is 돌아가다 ('to go the long way round'), and it pairs with the verb 질러가다 ('to cut across'), which shares the same 지르다 root. Register is neutral and everyday. The English-speaker pitfall: do not confuse 지름길 with 골목길 (alley) — an alley can serve as a shortcut, but 골목길 names the narrow street itself while 지름길 names the shorter route, whatever street it uses. Spelling also traps learners: it is 지름길, pronounced [지름낄], so people mishear and write 지름낄.

usage: at the fork in the road
examples: 갈림길에서 왼쪽으로 가세요.
At the fork, go left.
에서 marks the split point where the choice happens
조금 더 가면 갈림길이 나와요.
If you go a little further, a fork comes up.
나오다 = (a feature) appears ahead, the natural verb for terrain coming into view
지금 인생의 갈림길에 서 있는 기분이에요.
I feel like I'm standing at a crossroads in life right now.
the figurative use Koreans love — a big decision point, 인생의 갈림길
nuance: 갈림길 is a native compound from 갈리다 ('to be divided / to split') + 길 ('road'), so the picture is one path branching apart into two or more, the moment you must choose a direction. Literally it guides walking or driving (갈림길에서 오른쪽으로), but Koreans use it just as readily for life's decision points (인생의 갈림길 = a crossroads in life). Its key contrast is with 사거리 (a four-way intersection): a 갈림길 splits one road into branches like a Y, whereas a 사거리 is where two roads cross like a plus sign — splitting versus crossing. It pairs with 나오다 ('to come up ahead') and the locative 갈림길에서. Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfall: English 'crossroads' covers both the literal X-crossing and the figurative dilemma, so learners over-extend 갈림길 to a true intersection — but a road that crosses, not branches, is 교차로 or 사거리; reserve 갈림길 for a fork.

mistakes: Confusing 갈림길 (a fork that splits one road into branches) with 사거리 (a four-way intersection where two roads cross) — splitting is not the same as crossing
Spelling it 갈림낄 from the pronunciation — the written form is 갈림길

examples: 보도로 걸으세요.
Walk on the sidewalk.
the simplest safety instruction; 로 = along/by way of
보도가 좁아서 한 줄로 걸었어요.
The sidewalk was narrow, so we walked single file.
아서 = because; a real everyday observation about Korean sidewalks
자전거가 보도로 다녀서 위험할 뻔했어요.
A bike was riding on the sidewalk, so it was almost dangerous.
ㄹ 뻔했다 = nearly happened; the live issue of bikes on 보도
nuance: 보도 is Sino-Korean, 步道, literally 'step-road' (步 walk + 道 road) — the formal name for the pedestrian walkway beside a street, identical in meaning to 인도 (人道, 'person-road'). The dividing line between the two is register and channel: 보도 dominates official signage and traffic law (보도 침범 = encroaching on the sidewalk), while 인도 is what people more often say in casual speech; both are correct. Its true opposite is 차도 (車道, 'car-road', the roadway). The everyday compound 보도블록 (the tiled paving blocks) comes up constantly in complaints about uneven sidewalks. The big English-speaker pitfall is a homograph collision: another 보도 means 'news report' (報道, as in 언론 보도 = press coverage) — same hangul, different hanja — so a sentence about 보도 could be about pavement or the press, and only context tells them apart. Also note British 'pavement' = American 'sidewalk' = 보도; don't read it as the road surface.

usage: to go up onto the overpass
육교 usually means stairs to climb
examples: 육교로 건너세요.
Cross by the overpass.
the basic instruction; 로 = by way of
육교 계단이 많아서 좀 힘들었어요.
The overpass had a lot of stairs, so it was a bit tiring.
아서 = because; the real complaint about older 육교 with no elevator
횡단보도가 없어서 육교를 이용해서 길을 건넜어요.
There was no crosswalk, so I crossed the road using the overpass.
이용하다 = to make use of; the legal, safe way across when no crosswalk exists
nuance: 육교 is Sino-Korean, 陸橋, literally 'land-bridge' (陸 land + 橋 bridge) — a footbridge that carries pedestrians up and over a busy road. Its clean opposite is 지하도 (地下道), the underground passage you go down into; the memory hook is direction — 육교 you climb UP, 지하도 you go DOWN. Distinguish it sharply from 다리 (a plain bridge): a 다리 spans a river and usually carries cars (한강 다리), whereas a 육교 is specifically for people crossing over a road. Older 육교 have many stairs (육교 계단) and no elevator, so travelers with luggage or strollers grumble. It pairs with 건너다, 올라가다, 이용하다. The English-speaker pitfall: 'overpass' in English often means a road flyover for cars, but 육교 is for pedestrians — a car overpass over a road is 고가도로. So don't call the highway flyover a 육교, and don't call a river bridge a 육교 either.

usage: to go down into the underpass
examples: 지하도로 건너세요.
Cross via the underpass.
the basic direction; 로 = by way of
지하도로 내려가면 여름엔 시원해요.
If you go down into the underpass, it's cool in summer.
으면 = if; 내려가다 = go down — the natural verb because you descend into it
지하도 상가에서 양말이랑 우산을 샀어요.
I bought socks and an umbrella at the underground arcade.
이랑 = and (casual); 지하도 상가, the shops many underpasses house
nuance: 지하도 is Sino-Korean, 地下道, literally 'under-ground road' (地 ground + 下 below + 道 road) — the passage that takes pedestrians beneath a busy road or intersection. Its mirror image is 육교 (陸橋): 지하도 you go DOWN into, 육교 you climb UP over, same crossing by opposite directions. The trap synonym is 지하철 (地下鐵, 'underground iron' = subway): they share 지하 (underground) but 지하도 is a walking tunnel while 지하철 is the train — a 지하도 may connect to a 지하철역 but is not the same thing. Many large 지하도 double as 지하도 상가 (underground shopping arcades), so locals duck in both to cross and to browse. It pairs with 내려가다, 건너다, 출구. The English-speaker pitfall: English 'underground' alone is ambiguous (passage vs. subway), so learners say 지하 when they mean the passage — be specific: the walkway is 지하도, the subway is 지하철. Also use 내려가다 (go down), not 들어가다, to capture the descent.

usage: add 하다 to make the verb
examples: 여기서 우회전이에요.
It's a right turn here.
the clipped noun form a passenger says to a driver
사거리에서 우회전하세요.
Turn right at the intersection.
우회전하다 = to make a right turn; 에서 marks where the turn happens
우회전 차선으로 미리 들어가야 안 막혀요.
You have to get into the right-turn lane early so you don't get stuck.
미리 = in advance; real driving advice, 우회전 차선 = the right-turn lane

You hear it constantly from GPS apps like 카카오내비 and 티맵, and as a passenger you direct a taxi with 여기서 우회전해 주세요. nuance: 일방통행 is Sino-Korean, 一方通行, literally 'one-direction pass-go' (一 one + 方 direction + 通行 passage), describing a road where traffic may legally flow in only one direction — a constant feature of Korea's older, narrow neighborhood streets. Its conceptual opposite is two-way traffic, but be careful with the term: the standard word is 양방향 통행 (兩方向, 'both-directions') or simply 양방향, not the made-up 양방통행. Related is 역주행 (逆走行, driving against the flow), the violation you commit if you miss the sign. 일방통행 pairs with 도로, 길, 표지판, and the consequence verb 돌아가다 ('to go around the long way'). The English-speaker pitfall: don't model the antonym on the word and say 양방통행 — Koreans say 양방향. Also, 일방통행 governs the road itself, so it binds cyclists and motorbikes too, not just cars; and figuratively 일방통행 can describe a one-sided relationship (그 사랑은 일방통행이었다), a nuance worth recognizing.
